strengths: Well-motivated benchmark contribution: EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA addresses action recognition evaluation with hard, semantically similar distractors using SOTA models
Strong empirical results: 21-point improvement on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA (73.4% vs 52.2%), SOTA on original task (58.3%), and consistent improvements across 6+ benchmarks
Comprehensive experimental rigor: Proper OOD/IID distinction, thorough leave-one-out ablations, multiple baselines, and consistent evaluation protocols
Valuable insights on language representation: Quantitative evidence that narrations significantly outperform official keys (Table 8), with clear examples of label ambiguity
Methodologically complete: Well-motivated combination of techniques (vision supervision, temporal detection, prior actions, adversarial training) with thorough ablations
Strong reproducibility commitment: Code release promised, clear licensing information, extensive implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of individual methods: Vision token supervision, adversarial training, and auxiliary tasks are known techniques; main contribution is their combination for action recognition

Confounded experimental design: OOD evaluation uses AVION distractors (not TIM) to avoid IID, making it unclear how much improvement comes from hard negatives vs. auxiliary tasks; Table 7 shows AVION removal only costs 5.2 points
Modest improvements on standard task: Only 1.9-point improvement on original EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with official keys (58.3% vs 56.4%); headline 21-point improvement is on newly-constructed benchmark

Inconsistent experimental setup: Different frame counts (8/16/32/64) for different experiments, GPT-4o only at 8-frames, K=5 vs K=20 choices not justified, large-scale data augmentation (530K pairs) makes baselines less comparable

Benchmark construction limitations: Using TIM to generate distractors may bias toward its failure patterns; test set based on TIM's predictions limits neutrality; no analysis of cross-model applicability
Mixed generalization results: Performance changes inconsistent across other benchmarks (NextQA: -0.4%, VideoMME: +0.6%); suggests limited transfer of proposed techniques
Insufficient per-category analysis: No breakdown of improvements by action type on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA; unclear which actions benefit from proposed methods

Methodological specificity concerns: Vision token supervision tied to EPIC-KITCHENS-100's fixed classes; temporal detection padding may create train-test mismatch; prior action memory depends on unreliable model predictions

strengths: Clear identification of MLLM weaknesses in action recognition with difficult distractors
Useful benchmark contribution (EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA) that provides cleaner MQA-format evaluation
Strong empirical results on the proposed benchmark (73.4% accuracy, 21-point improvement over GPT-4o)
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 additional video benchmarks
Thorough ablation study (Table 7) and detailed appendix with qualitative analysis
Well-motivated problem addressing open-vocabulary and distractor difficulty issues
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: vision token supervision, temporal detection, and prior action memory are standard techniques (multi-task learning, prompt engineering) rather than novel methods
Benchmark design concerns: reliance on single SOTA model (TIM) for distractors creates potential bias; unclear if narrations are objectively better than official keys or just suit MLLMs better

Unclear contribution attribution: 530K additional training samples (including GPT-4o annotations) added alongside methods; no ablation isolating data augmentation effects from methodological contributions
Poor generalization: marginal improvements on other benchmarks (+0.4 to +2.5%), including performance degradation on NextQA (-0.4%), suggesting domain-specific overfitting to EPIC-KITCHENS-100
Inconsistent experimental setup: different frame counts across tables (8, 16, 32, 64), unfair GPT-4o comparison due to cost constraints, IID vs. OOD framing somewhat artificial

Insufficient analysis: Table 7 ablations show only 0.3-1.5% degradation per component (not justifying full complexity); missing analysis of which action types benefit from each method, computational costs, hyperparameter sensitivity
Questionable design choices without justification: why n=2 for prior actions, K=5/K=20 for MQA, 70/30 split for augmentation, uniform temporal padding distribution
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, multiple runs, or significance testing
Reproducibility concerns: code/models not available at submission; TIM uses non-commercial license; some implementation details vague

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: clearly demonstrates that MLLMs struggle with hard negative examples and proposes a novel solution using SOTA action recognition models (TIM, AVION) to generate challenging distractors

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 different video understanding benchmarks (EPIC-KITCHENS-100, EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, EgoSchema, PerceptionTest, LongVideoBench, VideoMME, MVBench) with detailed ablation studies
Strong empirical results: 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA (73.4% vs 52.2%) and state-of-the-art on original EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (58.3% accuracy)
Valuable insight about data representation: demonstrates that language simplification in official keys hurts MLLM performance compared to raw narrations (Table 8)
High reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, comprehensive methodology, code to be released, and both OOD and IID evaluation settings

Multiple complementary methods rather than single-technique approach: vision token supervision, temporal detection, adversarial training, egocentric prompting, and prior action memory work together effectively
Practical benchmark contribution: EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA will serve as a useful harder evaluation setting for action recognition in MLLMs
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: vision token supervision builds on concurrent work, temporal detection is standard auxiliary task, prior action memory is straightforward concatenation, egocentric prompting is prompt engineering. The contribution is primarily in combination rather than individual methods.

Unclear attribution between data augmentation and proposed methods: training uses 530K augmented pairs (vs 67K original), including narrations, adversarial distractors, and GPT-4o generations. Leave-one-out ablations show small individual contributions (1-5 points), making it unclear how much improvement comes from methods vs. data augmentation.

Benchmark design concerns: EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA test set generated using TIM's predictions, but TIM also used during training in IID setting. While OOD evaluation with AVION is provided, raises questions about whether improvements reflect better action understanding or better fitting to TIM's specific errors.

Limited generalization to diverse benchmarks: improvements on VideoMME minimal (+0.6%) with negative results on some categories (Multilingual: -6.7%), mixed results on LongVideoBench with many categories degrading. Results on additional benchmarks require mixing in external LLaVA-Video-178K data, suggesting approach may be domain-specific.

Distribution mismatch in prior action learning: uses ground truth previous actions during training but model predictions at test time. This significant mismatch only yields +0.5-0.7 point improvement, questioning the method's practical utility.

Incomplete method analysis: gap between 73.4% on 5-way MQA versus 58.3% on full classification task not fully explained. MQA is inherently easier. Connection between methods and performance on original task unclear.

Missing comparisons and analysis: only 2 action recognition baseline models (AVION, TIM); no learning curves; only 2 epochs of training without demonstrating convergence; no statistical significance testing with confidence intervals; limited explanation of why MLLMs struggle with action recognition fundamentally.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets and benchmarks (4 action recognition datasets, 13 MLLM benchmarks) with thorough ablations (additive, leave-one-out, token design variants)
Well-motivated problem: identifies genuine gap in MLLM fine-grained action understanding and proposes principled hard example mining solution using specialist models

Strong empirical results on action recognition benchmarks (SOTA on EPIC-KITCHENS-100, 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on custom benchmark) with good generalization across model scales and architectures
Rigorous methodological approach including OOD/IID separation with statistical validation (JSD analysis, p < 0.001) and careful handling of benchmark construction
Excellent reproducibility: detailed prompts, hyperparameters, 530K annotated video-language pairs, code/models promised, proper licensing documentation

Insightful analysis including attention-based investigation, difficulty level robustness (Table 8), and automatic discovery of challenging aspects (temporal order, similar objects) without explicit curation
weaknesses: Benchmark construction lacks human validation: hard distractors are assumed meaningful but no human evaluation confirms they capture important semantic distinctions vs. specialist model artifacts; circularity risk in training on AVION and testing on TIM

Limited architectural novelty: action token is straightforward learnable token with intermediate supervision; improvements predominantly from adversarial distractors (9.4 points) rather than architectural innovations; model designs are incremental over LLaVA-Video

Two-stage pipeline creates critical practical limitations: requires specialist model predictions at inference time, imposes arbitrary top-K constraint (K=20) limiting open-vocabulary capability, multi-round approach actually achieves better results (40%) but is computationally infeasible

Domain-specific generalization concerns: primarily evaluated on egocentric kitchen actions; marginal or negative improvements on diverse benchmarks (VideoMME, many categories in Table 7 show <1% gain or degradation); limited transfer validation beyond narrow domains

Unclear contribution attribution and training data composition: 530K pairs with unclear task type breakdown, heavy reliance on data replay with LLaVA-Video-178K makes isolating EPIC-KITCHENS improvements difficult, GPT-4o bias propagation from caption/QA generation not discussed

Hard example mining generalizability unvalidated: only EPIC-KITCHENS-100 used for benchmark construction; whether hard example mining strategy transfers to other action datasets unknown; limited evidence that discovered challenges (temporal order) are universally important

Inconsistent evaluation protocols: different frame counts across experiments (8f/16f/32f/64f), GPT-4o limited to 8 frames due to cost while LLaVAction uses more frames in some settings, confounding direct comparison and fairness assessment

strengths: Clear problem motivation: identifies genuine limitations of existing MLLM evaluation for action understanding (easy random distractors, free-text preventing fair comparison)
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets: EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA plus 4 action recognition benchmarks and 13 MLLM benchmarks; shows generalization across model sizes
Thorough ablation studies: Tables 3 and 11 systematically decompose contributions; additional variants in appendices
Thoughtful multi-perspective training design: combines adversarial distractors, temporal detection, temporal order learning, and direct prediction
Reproducibility commitment: detailed implementation details, prompts in appendices, promised code/data release
Hard example mining strategy is practical: using specialist models more efficient than human curation or closed-source MLLM annotation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: hard example mining is well-established (Shrivastava et al. 2016); action token is just auxiliary loss supervision (similar to CLS tokens); data reformulation combines existing task formats; two-stage pipeline is straightforward external filtering

Benchmark design concerns: no human validation of distractor semantic similarity; model-dependent construction creates circularity (tuning to specific models' failures); limited scope (kitchen videos only); Appendix F.1 reveals action labels themselves are ambiguous, suggesting benchmark difficulty may reflect poor formulation rather than genuine challenges
Overclaimed results: Table 7 shows most improvements ≤2.5 points, several negative; overall improvement across 10 benchmarks is +0.6 to +1.7 points; claims of 'strong improvements' are misleading

Impractical two-stage pipeline: requires specialist models at inference, defeating generalist MLLM purpose; creates dependency on models unavailable for new domains; Table 12 shows necessity but limits applicability

Experimental inconsistencies: different frame counts (8-64) across experiments; K scaled to 20 for EPIC-KITCHENS but 5 for others (dataset-specific tuning); GPT-4o comparisons limited to 8 frames while model uses more

Shallow analysis of learning: attention correlations (0.00769 vs 0.00476) lack statistical testing and interpretation; no error analysis; Table 8 shows performance degrades with difficulty, suggesting memorization not robust learning
OOD/IID confusion: paper argues for OOD (AVION train, TIM test) but Table 2 shows IID performs better (77.0 vs 74.1); JSD metric doesn't guarantee semantic OOD
Generalization concerns: zero-shot performance remains poor (Table 7); unclear why approach would work without specialist action models; VideoMME performance degrades without explanation

Training data confound: data replay mixes EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with general video data (LLaVA-Video-178K), making it unclear whether improvements come from action-specific learning or better general understanding
Questionable design choices lack justification: token position ordering not ablated; temporal padding δ=3 seconds not justified; 30% MQA ratio with prior action arbitrary

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Convincingly demonstrates that MLLMs struggle with fine-grained action understanding when facing semantically similar distractors
Novel and useful benchmark: EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA using hard example mining via specialist models is more efficient and principled than alternatives; thoughtful OOD/IID experimental design
Strong empirical results: 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on hard benchmark; SOTA on multiple action recognition datasets (58.3% on EPIC-KITCHENS-100); consistent improvements across diverse domains
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: Multiple datasets, 13 MLLM benchmarks, thorough ablations, attention analysis, and difficulty-level analysis demonstrating robustness
Practical and efficient design: Two-stage pipeline is 190× faster than alternatives; action token adds minimal overhead; demonstrations across multiple base models
Reproducibility and transparency: Code, data, models promised; detailed implementation details; good documentation of methodological choices and prompts
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Hard example mining is established; action token is similar to CLS token; multi-task training is standard—contribution is mainly in systematic combination rather than fundamental innovation

Marginal improvements on general MLLM benchmarks: Table 7 shows <2% gains on most tasks with some performance drops; VideoMME results are flat, suggesting limited generalization beyond action understanding

Heavy dependence on specialist models: Two-stage pipeline requires trained specialist model (TIM); creates distribution mismatch (GT in top-K during training but not at inference); complicates fair comparison

Data reformulation complexity: Heavy use of GPT-4o for captions/QAs shows degradation when used alone; mixing in-domain EPIC-KITCHENS and out-of-domain LLaVA-Video-178K data complicates attribution; domain-specific engineering reduces generalizability
Marginal contribution of action token: Only 0.3 point improvement in ablation (69.1 vs 68.8); 0.5 point drop in leave-one-out; added complexity not clearly justified

Single-source benchmark with limited scope: Constructed only on EPIC-KITCHENS-100; K=5 distractors is relatively small; inherits TIM's biases; generalization only demonstrated on domain-similar datasets

Experimental design concerns: Different frame counts for different models; GPT-4o not fine-tuned while LLaVAction extensively tuned on EPIC-KITCHENS-100; two-stage pipeline advantage unavailable to baselines; no significance testing or error bars

Over-engineered with fragmented contributions: Multiple components with independent benefits (largest is adversarial distractors at 9.4 points); unclear which components are essential vs. optional; dense presentation obscures main contributions
